The Arabic word Sakîna corresponds to the Hebrew Shekhinah, a concept of great importance in the Kabbalah and one that, broadly speaking, can be understood in Jewish religious consciousness as the personal embodiment, or hypostasis, of God's Presence in the world.
More directly, the Arabic word suggests stillness, trust, and gentleness. Its root, skn, carries the idea of dwelling in a home, of resting in a presence that brings quiet, peace, and security.

Quranic verses evoking this idea have received extensive commentary. One of them says: “Those who believe, and whose hearts find peace in the remembrance of God—yes, it is in the remembrance of God (dhikr Allâh) that their hearts find peace” (13:28). Stillness, peace: itmî’nân.

Another verse answers it: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord” (89:27–28). It is precisely this itmî’nân—the soul's serenity as an unshakable certainty of faith in what it has itself seen—that the Fifth Imam, Mohammad al-Bâqir, invokes when commenting on yet another verse: “It is God who sends down the sakîna into the hearts of believers, so that they may add faith to their faith” (48:4).

He goes on to explain that those upon whom the sakîna descends are the people spoken of in this verse: “He strengthens them [inspires them, gives them strength] with a Spirit from Himself” (58:22). They are also those described in the hadîth: “In my community there are those who speak, and there are those to whom [the angels] speak”—the mohaddathûn.

The central idea, then, is of a Presence that comes to dwell within the soul. For Sohrawardî, that Presence takes a particular form: blazing Lights, all those luminous phenomena (photisms) and revelations of light that he experienced before Najmoddîn Kobrâ and his school would describe similar experiences.

When these Lights reach their greatest intensity, they become steady and remain for a time. This is what is called the sakîna. Sohrawardî speaks of “those who possess the greater Sakîna” (al-Sakînat al-kobrâ). His commentators explain that he means “those in whom the spiritual Lights and the flashing radiances remain as a lasting presence.”

That is also why the passage quoted above, where the two currents of mystical leaven meet and join in the community of the Sakîna, opens into an account of the different states of the Light of Glory, the Zoroastrian Xvarnah. It is in the form of Sakîna-Xvarnah that the two mystical traditions come together among the Ishrâqîyûn.
Sohrawardî's conviction that this union establishes their spiritual ancestry opens a path not yet explored by comparative theology and the study of mysticism.

For the luminous Presence that comes to dwell in purified souls is the same Presence that invested and guided the blessed kings Fereydûn and Kay Khosraw. It is also the Presence that revealed itself to Moses, when a voice called to him from within the burning bush for a secret encounter (28:30).
And Kay Khosraw's experience becomes the model for the illumination of a soul that has itself become the burning bush.

So the ishrâqî interpretation reads the Quranic Verse of Light: “God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. This light is like a hearth containing a lamp, a lamp within crystal ... and it is light upon light” (24:35).

Of course, when Sohrawardî traces the ancestry of the Ishrâqîyûn in this way, he is not writing an objective history of philosophy or mysticism. He is describing the history of souls as he perceives it within the history of his own soul, where that history takes place.
It would therefore be quite beside the point for a historian to object that his picture of the past is a construction of the mind, simply because it does not fit neatly with our historical records.

Such an objection would miss the only history Sohrawardî means to tell: the history he himself brings into being and is, not as an outward sequence of deeds, but as something lived in the innermost depths of his being.

It is when his spiritual perception brings that history into the present that the predecessors gathered in his family tree truly become the predecessors of the Ishrâqîyûn: Sohrawardî himself is both the witness and the evidence.
Time is turned around. It is from his own present, where these earlier figures become part of his living story, that they come to be the predecessors of the Ishrâqîyûn.

This is the whole difference—as we have already suggested in Book I—between existential historicity, the way history is lived from within, and what is ordinarily called historical existence. Unfortunately, the first is sometimes overlooked in favor of the second.
We shall return to the distinction.
Having established what the spiritual ancestry of the Ishrâqîyûn means, we may now hope to reach, with them, what Sohrawardî calls the “Eastern source.”
First, we must approach it by asking what this “Eastern” knowledge is, and what entitles its possessors to be called “Eastern” sages.

As we have already had occasion to explain (in Book I), the words hikmat and hokamâ, though often translated as “philosophy” and “philosophers,” are not adequately rendered by either term. “Theology” and “theologians” would be no more suitable. Hikmat and hokamâ belong to a different order from scholastic theology (Kalâm) and the scholastic theologians of Islam (Motakallimûn). Nor is hikmat simply philosophy combined with theological debate. The closest translation would be “wisdom” (sophia), provided we understand wisdom in its deepest spiritual sense: a wisdom touched by direct mystical knowledge, such as the ecstatic vision of Kay Khosraw will reveal to us (see Chapter IV).

We must not understand it merely in the ordinary sense of practical wisdom or knowledge gained through life. Even the adjective “sapiential,” derived from the Latin sapientia (wisdom), no longer conveys clearly enough its original connection with sapere: to taste, savor, experience—the dhaoq spoken of in our texts. For the thinkers we are studying, knowledge draws upon three sources, each recognized as valid within its own sphere.

First comes tradition (naql), which nourishes theology. Second comes the intellect (’aql), the instrument of philosophical reasoning, whether in Kalâm or in falsafa, the Arabic adaptation of the Greek philosophia. Finally comes what we may broadly call “spiritual perception,” or direct knowledge of the sacred (kashf, literally “unveiling” or “discovery”). This last is the source of the knowledge that constitutes divine wisdom (hikmat ilâhîya) and mystical gnosis (’irfân). Naturally, mystical gnosis does not disregard the first two sources. It presupposes them, just as the inner, esoteric meaning (bâtin) presupposes the outward, exoteric meaning (zâhir).

When Sohrawardî and his companions speak of the hakîm ilâhî, the “divine sage” or “sage of God,” they are therefore using what is, as we should recall, an exact equivalent of the Greek theosophos. Hikmat ilâhîya, or often simply hikmat, is Theo-sophia—divine wisdom in the original meaning of the word. “Eastern Theosophy” (ishrâqîya) is the wisdom of someone who unites the highest speculative understanding with the deepest spiritual experience.

Indeed, that experience can itself be called “speculative” in the word's original sense: it transforms the sage into a speculum, a pure mirror in which the pure Lights rising from the East of the spiritual world are reflected and by which the sage is set ablaze. This is the foundation upon which the hierarchy of “Eastern” sages will be established (see § 2 below).

The perfect “Eastern” sage is a hakîm mota’allih. He is not simply a mystic whose experience resembles that of many mystics without philosophical training, or of those who believe such training unnecessary or even dangerous. Nor is he merely a philosopher, like so many others who know nothing of putting philosophy into spiritual practice, of realizing its truth in their own being. The complete spiritual experience of this “theosopher”—this sophos, or sage of divine Sophia—may be described as an experience of divine Wisdom itself.

We must now examine more closely the technical meaning of the terms Sohrawardî uses when he speaks of ta’alloh, the spiritual state of the hakîm mota’allih. The word ta’alloh—formed from the Arabic root ’lh in its fifth verbal form—carries two related meanings. It denotes both becoming godlike, or assuming a divine form, and worship or devoted service to the divinity. In its first sense, it corresponds to theôsis, the term used by Byzantine mystics in Sohrawardî's own time.

Yet if we meditate carefully upon that particularly revealing part of his work consisting of his “tales of initiation” and his “Book of Hours,” we are led to understand his intentions by following a path he himself opened a few pages earlier, when we sought to clarify what he meant by the word “Magi.”

We can follow that path here because he refers to the teachings and exemplary experiences of Zoroaster and Plato. Within his “Eastern Theosophy,” these two names also point toward the Chaldaean Oracles and the Neoplatonic sages. What Sohrawardî calls ta’alloh seems, in fact, to have much in common with what the later Neoplatonists called theurgy. His mota’allih, the sage who has undergone this transformation, shares many characteristics with the figure they called the theurgic or “hieratic” sage. Indeed, the “hieratic” is a category that embraces Sohrawardî's entire vision of the world: in that vision, every species is the “theurgy,” the “hieratic work,” of its Angel.

The Greek word theourgos appears to have been coined by the “Chaldaeans” who composed the Oracles, toward the end of the second century. Proclus and his school use the name “theurgic sages” collectively for these “Chaldaeans”: all the members of the mystical community known by that rather imprecise name, whose teaching the Neoplatonists themselves brought back to life. Whereas theologians are “those who speak of divine things,” theurgists are “those who bring about divine things.” This distinction corresponds exactly to the one Sohrawardî so carefully establishes between the philosopher as such and the hakîm mota’allih. The “divine work” can be understood in several ways. Theurgy may be called a divine work because it confers a divine nature upon the human being through the “sacrament of immortality” at the heart of Chaldaean teaching and initiation.

Yet insofar as this making-immortal (apathanatismos) appears as the “offspring” of a deification (apothéôsis), the word theurgy also takes on the metaphysical meaning given to it by the Neoplatonic philosophers. For Iamblichus and Proclus alike, the human intellect is incapable of perceiving the supreme God in the perfection of his nature. Its power extends to the contemplation of the Ideas in their multiplicity, but not to their source: the undivided unity of the Noêton, the intelligible—or rather the supra-intelligible—in its absolute oneness. That supreme goal can be reached only through a higher faculty of perception, the “flower of the intellect.”

What takes place is no longer an act of intellectual reasoning. It is the result of a state beyond reason: a living flame kindled in the soul by divine Light, just as a flower is a flame drawn from the depths of the earth by the sun's warmth. As the philosopher Damascius observes, this gnosis, which must be apprehended through the “flower of thought,” is “not an impetuous knowledge; it does not struggle with its object; it does not hurry to seize possession of it; rather, it surrenders itself to it.” This cognitio passiva, this receptive knowledge, marks the state of union (enôsis) described by Plotinus. In different formulations, the gnostics and Sufis of Islam would say much the same thing in their attempts to express the moment when consciousness becomes aware of the presence of the divine Subject—the true subject of the activities taking place within that consciousness.

It is precisely a power of the same kind that enables Sohrawardî's sage to attain the supreme vision of the “Light of Glory.” The Neoplatonists call this power theurgic, and the Chaldaean Oracles present it as a necessary condition for the soul's ascent (anagôgê).

Thus, among the Neoplatonists, theurgy can mean both a practical method of active union (drastikê enôsis) with spiritual beings and the union beyond reason in which the Subject performing the “divine work” is the divine Subject himself. This “method” is also called hieratic, and those who practice it are the “hieratics.” For the Neoplatonists, Chaldaean theurgy was one hieratic method, though not the only one. Such a method always rests upon certain ascetic disciplines and presupposes a whole body of theosophical knowledge. Iamblichus seems to have borrowed the term hieratic from the Hermeticists. In any case, when he affirms the superiority of the hieratic life over that of the philosopher alone, he establishes exactly the same precedence that Sohrawardî gives to the hakîm mota’allih within the mystical hierarchy of sages whose ancestry goes back to Hermes.

The expressions in which the adjective “hieratic” occurs help us understand it more precisely. There is, for example, a “hieratic hope.” One of the Chaldaean Oracles declares: “Hope filled with fire shall be your nourishment.” Hope here is a faculty of spiritual intelligence, an instrument of knowledge. The same is true of everything in the Oracles qualified by a compound containing the word “fire,” for such expressions indicate a gift descending from the supreme Intelligence. This “hieratic hope,” like hope more generally in the language of the mystery communities, such as that of Eleusis, means the initiate's trust in a blessed life beyond death. It lies at the heart of the “sacrament of immortality” practiced by the Chaldaean Magi, and it accords entirely with the teaching of Sohrawardî and the “Neoplatonists of Persia.”

The theurgic or hieratic ascent of the soul (anagôgê) was therefore the central mystery of the sacramental community whose sacred book was the Chaldaean Oracles. Its teaching offered more than knowledge about a mystery. The purpose of the sacrament, the mystery (teletê, mysterion), and of initiation itself (teleiôsis), was to render the soul immortal. What Proclus and a few others tell us about the teaching of the “hieratics” is that they sought to separate the soul from its physical body before the final departure of death, before the exitus. The aim was to give the soul the capacity to break the bonds tying it to the body and to physical nature. Here we should recall the kinship between two Greek words: teleutân, to die, and teleisthai, to be initiated. The soul has descended temporarily into this world to fulfill the mission and role assigned to it as a soul. That mission can be completed only if the soul is capable of ascending once more to the place from which it descended.

But this requires the soul, carried by its subtle vehicle alone (okhêma), to have become accustomed to separating itself from its physical body while it still inhabits that body. Otherwise, it risks being overwhelmed by the violence of physical death. The Greek terms for the soul's double movement of descent and return (kathodos and épanodos) have exact equivalents in the terminology of Islamic mystical theosophy: the two arcs of nozûl and so’ûd. The conviction that mystical death must come before physical death, so that physical death may be rendered harmless, is so compelling that its commandment is placed upon the lips of the Prophet himself in a hadith: “Die before you die...” In the seventeenth century, the great Shiite philosopher and spiritual master Mîr Dâmâd would repeat Sohrawardî's own words: “No one is truly a mota’allih, a hieratic sage, until he has made himself capable of taking off his physical body as one takes off a tunic.” Whether one speaks in Greek of khôrismos, separation, or in Arabic of tajarrud, one is speaking of exactly the same thing.

We need not imagine that this necessarily involves phenomena we would today regard as “disturbing” or “abnormal.” We have only to consider how often the mystical theosophers of Islam quoted the famous account of Plotinus's ecstasy, which they knew through the Arabic text of the work called the Theology of Aristotle (the beginning of that account will appear later in this book). That is the kind of experience at issue. The soul's ascent is also described in several surviving fragments of the Chaldaean Oracles, each of which may be understood as an account of the “sacrament of the soul's immortalization.” What we encounter is a drama mystikon, a mystical drama that can be expressed only through narrative. The same is true of Sohrawardî's “tales of initiation”: that is precisely what they seek to convey.

We also find a remarkable form of it in certain traditions attributed to the Imams of Shiism, notably the hadith of the “White Cloud,” interpreted by Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî (see Book V, Chapter III). All this also resonates with the text known as the “Mithras Liturgy” and with Apuleius's account of the mysteries of Isis. The action of the theurgic sacrament seeks to represent the destiny awaiting the initiate's soul after its physical exitus. This is also the purpose of Sohrawardî's Tale of the Western Exile. It is the story of the soul's passion: descent and return, death and rebirth. As Proclus says, citing one of the oracles: “The souls that have known the works of the Father”—the Ideas and the spiritual worlds—“escape the fatal wing of Destiny.” “Theurgists no longer belong to the herd of men subject to Destiny.”

But we must not misunderstand: supreme salvation is not accomplished by the hieratic sage acting alone. It would take a profound ignorance of humanity's religious history to accept, as some contemporary theology would have us do, that Christianity differs from other religions because salvation in Christianity is God's work, while other religions supposedly represent humanity's efforts to secure salvation for itself. The entire spirituality of Islamic gnosis, and indeed of Islam generally, bears witness against so simplistic a contrast.

Moreover, the Neoplatonic piety whose affinity with that of the shaykh al-Ishrâq we are considering also shows that the hieratic sage does not unite with spiritual beings without their assistance. This is all the more true when the theurgist—the one performing the “divine work”—is the divine Subject himself.

Proclus knows that “only someone possessing an angelic soul is capable of performing the hieratic operation,” although he keeps secret the nature of the sacrament that bestows this quality upon the soul. The reason is precisely that the quality is conferred by a ray of divine Light at the very moment when the soul's hieratic ascent culminates in mystical union with that Light. Proclus knows the hierarchy of Angels who “set the soul aflame with divine fire.” He speaks of the Angel who is the “guide of separation”: the guide who leads the soul out of the physical body. This Angel resembles the one who appears to Sohrawardî at the beginning of his Tales. For their part, the Chaldaean Oracles know the Angels as “beings of spiritual intelligence” who descend from the Empyrean at the supreme God's command to assist the hieratic soul. It is for this reason that the soul, as an “angel in potential,” has its dwelling among them after death, in the “angelic realm.”

Nevertheless, this hieratic operation—this ecstatic separation that anticipates the departure of death—can only announce itself and be experienced as the end of things and of time: as an individual event of the Last Things, an individual eschaton. This is exactly how it occurs in Sohrawardî.

We shall see it later in the account of Hermes's ecstasy, where Hermes appears as the hero of this ecstatic encounter with the end. This is why the shaykh al-Ishrâq so aptly describes the experience of the hieratic mystic, the mota’allih, by borrowing the expression “Great Upheaval” or “Great Shaking” (al-tâmmat al-kobrâ). In a Quranic verse, this expression announces the final hour, the eschaton. The theme is heard at the opening of the Tale of the Western Exile (see Chapter VI below), just as it appears in the visions of light described at the end of the Eastern Theosophy.

The preceding pages have tried to bring ta’alloh, mystical apothéosis, understood as the distinctive gift of the hieratic theosopher (mota’allih), into relation with the teachings of those whom Sohrawardî himself invokes in support of his own experience: the sages of Persia and Chaldaea, Zoroaster and Plato, as they appear within the traditions of Magian-Chaldaean spirituality and later Neoplatonism. We can now recognize in this mota’allih a spiritual companion of the theurgic or “hieratic” sage of the Chaldaean Oracles and the Neoplatonists.

But for our shaykh al-Ishrâq, this same theosopher is, by that very fact, the ishrâqî sage: the “Eastern” sage. This last characteristic marks the whole of his teaching and school. A Persian work written in seventeenth-century India, the Dabestân al-madhâhib (see also Book IV below), makes the point when it speaks of the Ishrâqîyân-e Irân, the “Eastern” theosophers of Iran—in other words, the “Platonists of Persia.”

We must now identify, in Sohrawardî's work, the qualities that distinguish the hieratic sage as an “Eastern” or ishrâqî theosopher. To understand the meaning and ideal of Ishrâq, we have briefly surveyed the spread of Magian spirituality westward and southwestward, in its “Chaldaean” and Neoplatonic forms. Sohrawardî's own explicit statements about Ishrâq will now allow us to recover, with him, the connection that was never entirely broken between the Chaldaean Magianism of the “Eastern-minded” Neoplatonists and the specifically Iranian Zoroastrian tradition stemming from the Avesta, its sacred book. The path of Ishrâq, of “Eastern” knowledge, is the path by which Sohrawardî invites us to rediscover with him the “Eastern Source”: that Light of Glory (Xvarnah, Khorrâh) which is the key to Zoroastrian cosmology and spirituality. For our shaykh, the Light of Ishrâq (Nûr ishrâqî, Lux orientalis) is identical with that Light of Glory.

For Sohrawardî, the word ishrâqî, “Eastern,” describes both the highest form of spiritual knowledge and the community of sages and theosophers—the “hieratics”—whose aim and vocation is to attain it. The word carries many layers of meaning. “East” and “Eastern” are not simply geographical or ethnic descriptions. Above all, they refer to something that cannot be located on the maps in our atlases.

We must therefore find a way to pass from the literal meaning of “East” to its spiritual meaning. What opens that passage is the idea of illumination: the appearance and vision of light, the experience of light itself.

Yet “illumination” alone is not enough to convey the reference to the Eastern source. Conversely, whenever we use the words “East” and “Eastern,” we must guard against a geographical misunderstanding. From the ishrâqî point of view, especially today, we must acknowledge that the geographical East is populated by great numbers of “Westerners,” while a few genuine “Easterners” still survive in the West. We should take our guidance from the statement quoted earlier: “Among the ancient Persians there was a community of chosen people guided by God.” In saying this, Sohrawardî had given a new application to a Quranic verse. If we can repeat this transformation of meaning, it will provide us with a criterion not only for recognizing the ancestors of the Ishrâqîyûn, but also for recognizing their successors: the “Eastern” tradition that alone entitles these sages to be called “Eastern.”

Let us begin with the passage in which the word Ishrâq first appears in Sohrawardî's great work, a passage that his two principal commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî and Shahrazôrî, expand upon in almost identical terms. Sohrawardî has just mentioned how insistently his friends, his “brothers,” urged him to commit to writing this “Eastern Theosophy,” whose inspiration, as he tells us at the end of the work, came to him “all at once, on a wonderful day.” Qotboddîn pauses over the two words that form the book's title. “These words,” he writes, “mean the theosophy founded upon the East of the Lights (Ishrâq, the light of the East), which is spiritual perception (kashf); or else the theosophy of the Easterners (mashâriqa), meaning the inhabitants of Persia (Ahl Fârs).

“In fact, the two meanings amount to the same thing, since the theosophy of the ancient Persians was a spiritual perception experienced through inward tasting (kashfîya dhawqîya). It therefore originated in the East of the Lights (Ishrâq), the East that is the manifestation (zohûr) of the pure Lights or pure Intelligences. It arose from their radiance and from the outpouring of the illuminations (ishrâqât) that dawn upon souls withdrawn from their physical bodies. The foundation of the ancient Persians' theosophy was inward experience and spiritual perception. The same was true of the ancient Greek sages, with the exception of Aristotle and his school, who relied upon rational debate and logical demonstration, and nothing else.”
Three lessons emerge from this passage.

1) The first concerns the spiritual meaning of the word East. The East, the light rising in the East, the hour of Ishrâq, is the primordial manifestation or revelation of being. It is the spiritual perception that takes place within consciousness when this Light flashes forth, disclosing the mystery of how being shines through into appearance. In the same way, the rising sun reveals the presence of things through the light of its dawn. The heavenly body rising in the physical sky, and the hour of its rising, correspond within the physical world to the moment when Knowledge dawns—and when the subject of that Knowledge awakens to itself, rising at its own East. The term ishrâq thus has a precise technical meaning that sets “Eastern” theosophy apart from every other kind. Just as, in the world of the senses, it names the splendor of morning, the instant when the sun's first brilliance unfolds in the crimson of the rising dawn, so, in the spiritual heaven of the soul, it names the revelatory moment of self-knowledge.

2) In a second sense, we may understand it as the theosophy of the Easterners: people whose home lies in the geographical East. We are told that these were the ancient Persians, the people of Fârs, of Persia.

Yet this involves no ethnic privilege whatsoever. Living in the East, or even being Persian, is not enough to make someone an “Easterner.” What qualifies the “Eastern” theosopher, the ancient Persian sage, is a different kind of investiture. It is announced by the words “East” and “Eastern” when these, like Ishrâq itself, are understood at the level of their spiritual meaning: the level at which the rising sun in the physical sky corresponds symbolically to the sun rising in the spiritual Heaven.

For as Qotboddîn observes, if the theosophy of the Easterners and Eastern theosophy amount to the same thing, it is because the wisdom of the ancient Persians was precisely that higher mystical theosophy known to us through the visionary perceptions of Kay Khosraw and Zarathustra, and through their teachings concerning the Xvarnah and the world of the archangelic Lights. Without this, the two expressions would not mean the same thing. The ancient Persians were therefore “Easterners” because their knowledge arose from that East. In other words, it is “Eastern” knowledge that makes a sage an “Eastern” theosopher; belonging by birth to the geographical East is not enough to make one's knowledge “Eastern.” Once their spiritual calling is understood in this way, the ancient Persian sages can rightly be regarded as the ancestors of the “Eastern” theosophy that Sohrawardî explicitly set out to revive.

3) These spiritual “Easterners” also happened, in the persons of the ancient Persian sages, to be geographically Eastern. It would therefore be especially absurd to separate what is supposedly the theosophy of Ishrâq—an “illuminative” theosophy—on the one hand, from the theosophy of the Easterners on the other (see p. 27 above). Our philosophers never made such a division. Avicenna himself had pursued an “Eastern philosophy.” Sohrawardî, who was better placed than we are to judge, explained why Avicenna's attempt had failed and why it was he, the shaykh al-Ishrâq, who had brought this Eastern philosophy into being. There is more. As we have already seen in tracing the spiritual genealogy, there is no reason to set the Greeks against the “Easterners.” The ancient Greek sages were also “Easterners,” because they too had access to the sources of higher mystical theosophy. The real opposition is between the “Easterners” and the Peripatetics of Aristotle's school, especially the “modern” Peripatetics of the Islamic world. These, together with the scholastic theologians of Kalâm, were Sohrawardî's principal adversaries.

The two terms East and Eastern (Ishrâq and Ishrâqî) bring three distinct visions together in a single culminating vision. There is the rising sun, with the hour and place of its rising. There is illumination, the morning splendor pouring forth from that East. And there is the rising sun itself. We may therefore speak of a knowledge that is Eastern because it is itself the East of knowledge; a knowledge that is illuminative because it is Eastern, and Eastern because it is illuminative. This is because such Knowledge is the very dawning of Knowledge, its morning, its hour of Ishrâq. It is the primordial place of Knowledge, the East from which all knowledge rises.

And finally, it is Knowledge that constitutes the very essence of the knowing Subject: the Subject's self-knowledge, which causes everything knowable to rise at its own East. The “Eastern” theosopher is an ishrâqî because to know is, for him, to be present to himself—and thus, by that very fact, to be present at the morning, at the East of knowledge. Conversely, his knowledge is “Eastern” because that presence makes his own self-present being the East from which the knowledge dawns. “Eastern” describes both a way of being and a way of knowing, each inseparable from the other.

We could multiply expressions in an attempt to make up for the inadequacy of any single translation. We might think of Jacob Boehme's aurora consurgens, the rising dawn, or of expressions found in Hegel: Eastern light, dawning light, the substance of dawn; or again, the essence of the rising sun, emerging light—Eastern light!—the substance of the East, the pure luminous essence of dawn. All this is contained in Ishrâq and “Eastern” theosophy. These expressions also harmonize with one already found in Latin Hermeticism: cognitio matutina, knowledge “at morning.” Everything before that morning is merely groping and illusion in the Darkness.

Thus, in its very title, Sohrawardî's theosophy gives form to its most beautiful symbol, one that brings with it the whole traditional symbolism of Light and Darkness. All the sages of the “Eastern” lineage have accordingly spoken in a language of signs and symbols (romûz). When we use the word “symbol” here, however, we mean neither an emblem or abstract sign nor an innocent allegory. We mean the forms assumed by an intermediate world, through which alone we can begin to apprehend the worlds above it. More precisely, we must speak of worlds that symbolize one another. In such a relationship, the symbol receives its truth from the higher reality it symbolizes; and what is an inner, esoteric spiritual truth at one level of meaning becomes an outward, exoteric truth at a higher level of being. The essential function of the symbol here is to initiate us into the mysteries.

“For everything I set forth concerning knowledge of the pure Lights—or beings of Light,” writes Sohrawardî, “and for everything founded upon that knowledge, as indeed for the rest of my teaching, I have the support of all those who have walked upon the path of God. For this higher knowledge was the inward experience (dhawq) of Plato, the Imam and leader of wisdom, a man endowed with great spiritual strength and inner light. Long before him, from Hermes, the father of the sages, down to Plato himself, it had also been the experience of other eminent philosophers, pillars of theosophical wisdom, such as Empedocles, Pythagoras, and others.

“Now the doctrines of those ancient sages were expressed in the language of symbols; arguments directed against them therefore do not refute them. Even when someone claims to argue against the outward, exoteric appearance (zâhir) of their doctrines, that person has not reached their true intentions at all, for symbols cannot be refuted in that way. It was precisely upon symbolism that the original Eastern doctrine of Light and Darkness was founded. This was the highest teaching of the sages of ancient Persia, such as Jâmâsp, Frashaoshtra, Bozorgmehr, and others before them. It was not the doctrine upon which the impiety of the dualist Magi (Majûs) was founded, nor was it the deviation of Mânî.”

This passage, particularly its final qualification, confirms what we have already seen. The book's two great commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî and Shahrazôrî, who here largely repeat one another, expand upon it in the following terms:

“It was upon symbolism that the doctrine of the Easterners (ahl al-Sharq) was founded—that is, the doctrine of the sages of ancient Persia, who professed the existence of two principles (asl), one Light and the other Darkness. These are, in fact, the respective symbols of necessary being and non-necessary being. Light stands for (qâ’im maqâm) Necessary Being; Darkness stands for non-necessary being. This does not mean that the absolutely First Principle divides into two principles, one Light and the other Darkness. No penetrating mind has ever maintained such a thing, least of all the elite of the Persian sages (fozalâ’ Fârs), who explored the depths of the sciences of being. That is why our Prophet, Mohammad, said in their praise: ‘Even if knowledge were suspended from the Pleiades, there would be men of Persia who would reach it.’ It is precisely their higher sciences and teachings that the author, Sohrawardî, has brought back to life in this book.

“The same was also the inward experience of the elite of the Greek sages, for the two communities, Persian and Greek, agreed upon the principle. Among the Persians were, for example, those named by the author: Jâmâsp, the disciple of Zoroaster; Frashaoshtra; and, most recently, Bozorgmehr. Their predecessors included King Gayômart, Tahmuras, Fereydûn, Kay Khosraw, and Zoroaster, among the great kings and prophets of high rank. It is true that the changing fortunes of history destroyed their higher sciences. The most disastrous blow was the loss of their sovereignty and Alexander's burning of most of their books.

“But the author succeeded in discovering certain aspects of their teachings. Finding that these agreed with what spiritual perception and intuitive vision (kashfîya shohûdîya) disclose, he recognized their excellence and worked to bring them to completion.”

This was how Sohrawardî's commentators assessed his work in the thirteenth century. The final remark in the passage they have just commented upon, with its reference to the Magi and to Mânî, is especially significant. Because Sohrawardî's concern is an “Eastern” knowledge, for which he claims an “Eastern” ancestry identified with that of ancient Persia, he found it necessary to guard against confusion. An earlier statement of his already gave us occasion to clarify which Magi he wished to distance himself from (see p. 29 above). They were, above all, the Magi who professed a radical dualism, and especially those among them who had entered into alliance with Ahriman.

We shall see in Chapter III that the great event of Sohrawardî's spiritual life was a visionary experience that transformed both his consciousness and his understanding of reality. It shattered, for him, the overly restrictive framework of the Aristotelian theory of the Intelligences. It was also the source of his interpretation of the Platonic Ideas through the language of Zoroastrian angelology. He appeals to the ecstatic visions of the prophet of ancient Persia as confirmation of his own vision, because he is convinced that Zoroaster did not belong to those who professed a radical dualism: the doctrine of two coeternal Principles, existing from the very beginning and on the same level of being, one a primordial Power of Light, the other a primordial opposing Power of Darkness.

We have just seen how Sohrawardî and his commentators tell us the true meaning to be given to the duality of principles in cosmogony and cosmology. The shaykh al-Ishrâq would maintain this interpretation consistently, for it is inseparable from the declaration whose significance we previously described as that of a manifesto: “Among the ancient Persians there was a community of chosen people guided by God, who walked upon the right path: eminent sages and theosophers bearing no resemblance to the Magi.” For our part, we can use the word “Magi” if we qualify it carefully enough to remove the associations that make it suspect.

Writing in Arabic, Sohrawardî could hardly give the word majûs any meaning other than the one current in the Islamic world. He therefore preferred another term, speaking of the Khosrawânîyûn. Earlier we encountered the “Platonic Magi.” Thanks to Sohrawardî, the connection between them and their Iranian ancestry was restored. By bringing about this “resurrection” of ancient Persian theosophy, he could, by that very act, claim an Iranian ancestry for his own theosophy, which he accordingly named ishrâqî, “Eastern.” From his time onward, the past was no longer what it had been: time had become reversible. That is precisely what the word “resurrection” implies.

Thus the resurrection of Zoroastrian theosophy within ishrâqî spirituality became conceivable in Islam through, and for, Sohrawardî—a thinker who himself professed the esoteric tawhîd, the affirmation of the One as uniquely One, and for whom the shadow of Ahriman was experienced as definitively overcome. Symbolic interpretation (ta’wîl) brings the two Principles back to two ontological aspects of being: on the one hand, Necessary Being, which possesses its full positivity by its very nature; on the other, non-necessary being, whose degree of potentiality measures its negativity.

Certainly, Sohrawardî's symbolic interpretation (ta’wîl) presupposes a modification of classical Mazdean dualism, if it does not itself accomplish that modification. But this change had precedents. The passage from Sohrawardî quoted above, together with his commentators' elaboration, invites us to extend our inquiry in three directions. Here we can do no more than indicate them briefly: 1) the efforts to overcome metaphysical dualism; 2) the figure of Zoroaster; and 3) the case of Mânî.

1) The classical Iranian form in which radical dualism appears to have been overcome is known as Zurvanism. Zervân, Unlimited Time, is understood as the original absolute divinity, from whose thought two “sons” proceed. Ohrmazd, the principle of Light, is born from Zervân's triumphant thought; Ahriman, the principle of Darkness, is born from the doubt, the negativity, that obscures Zervân's thought.

Yet this way of overcoming dualism still places two antagonistic Principles on the same level of being. Light and Darkness remain equal; indeed, it may even give Ahriman an immediate precedence, postponing Ohrmazd's reign until the end of the cosmic cycle. Such a solution was unacceptable to the gnostics of Islam. Consequently, when we detect traces of Zurvanism in their thought, what we actually find is something like a “neo-Zurvanism.” It is achieved through a radical alteration of the original Zurvanist drama, preserving the supremacy and primordial priority of the Principle of Light. Zervân is no longer the Supreme Principle but one of the beings of Light, one of the highest-ranking Angels of the Pleroma, the fullness of the angelic world. Darkness is therefore born not from the original Light itself, but from a being derived from that Light.

Nevertheless, one characteristic feature of Zurvanism is retained. A thought of doubt, a kind of vertigo before nothingness, takes hold of the Angel Zervân and, through him, gives birth to the Other, to Ahrimanian Darkness. This is how Shahrastânî describes the cosmogony of the Gayômartian gnostics, named after Gayômart, who appears sometimes as the Primordial Man and sometimes as one of the legendary rulers of the Iranian epic.

The same dramatic alteration appears, with the necessary differences, in the cosmogony and cosmology of the Oracles, or Logia, of the Chaldaean Magi (already discussed above, p. 32), and in their interpretation by the Neoplatonists. Once Evil and Darkness are understood as originating in a catastrophe within the angelic Pleroma, there is no longer any need to profess a radical metaphysical dualism. The principle of metaphysical monism—the ultimate unity of reality—is preserved. By accepting the Platonic principle that matter is divinely created, the Chaldaean Magi accepted the principle of a single-source explanation of the world's origin. They were not the Majûs whose impiety Sohrawardî condemned.

Yet once the catastrophe is admitted, whether the chief of the demons is called Ahriman or identified with Hades, and insofar as these demons correspond to the lower, irrational part of the soul, dualism at the human level becomes all the more powerful. The opposition between the faithful of Ohrmazd and the followers of Darkness reaches its greatest intensity in the struggle between the devout theurgists—the “hieratics,” assisted by the Angels, the Avestan Yazatas—and the goêtes, the Ahrimanian magicians assisted by demonic powers, the Devs. There can be little doubt that these Magi, reduced to the status of magicians who exploit the ambiguity of dualism, belong to the category of Majûs whose impiety Sohrawardî condemned, and who had made the very name Majûs suspect.

Hence the need, through vigilant moral conduct and ascetic discipline, to protect the conditions of the “hieratic ascent” against the snares of their demonology. Otherwise there is the danger of another catastrophe, traces of which can be found even in Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parsifal. There we read that Klingsor, the fallen knight who turned to black magic, had been initiated “in Persia” into the ars magica, the magical arts.

We must also recall that the “neo-Zurvanist” cosmology of the Gayômartians corresponds, point for point, to the “drama in Heaven” described in Ismaili Shiite cosmogony. Here too the Angel Zervân is represented as the third Intelligence of the Pleroma, the Spiritual Adam. His vertigo of doubt causes him to fall to the rank of tenth Intelligence, whereupon he becomes the demiurge of our world, creating it so that those who belong to him may find in it a means of salvation.

There is more. This characteristic seems to express so deeply and persistently a concern of the Iranian soul that we find it again in a major Twelver Shiite thinker of seventeenth-century Safavid Persia, Sayyed Ahmad ’Alawî. He was the student and son-in-law of the great Mîr Dâmâd (d. 1631), the intellectual master of several generations of Iranian philosophers. Using a commentary on Avicenna as his starting point, he constructed a monumental work entitled The Key to the Book of Healing (Miftâh Kitâb al-Shifâ’). He explicitly explains his choice of title by referring to Avicenna's mention of his “Eastern philosophy” in the prologue to that great book. For Sayyed Ahmad ’Alawî, the key is precisely this “Eastern philosophy.” When he comes to explain Avicenna's theory of multiplicity, he invokes the Pythagorean principle, “When the One emanates from the Cause, the non-One emanates from it also,” and immediately refers to “the teaching attributed to Zoroaster.” This teaching is, in fact, the very “neo-Zurvanism” discussed above. We have examined this ishrâqî testimony elsewhere and shall not dwell on it here.

2) We have seen how carefully Sohrawardî and his commentators distinguish Zoroaster and the sages of ancient Persia from the dualist Magi. We have also considered the spread of Iranian Magian spirituality toward the southwest, where it encountered “Chaldaean” wisdom and, ultimately, Neoplatonic wisdom. Although the Neoplatonists recognized an identity, or at least a definite affinity, between the doctrine of the Chaldaean Oracles and the doctrine believed to have been professed by the Magi of Zoroaster, some ancient authors were struck by differences suggesting two distinct personalities. They were therefore led to distinguish Zoroaster, the Persian prophet, from Zaratos—or Zoradès, or some similarly named figure—the Chaldaean Magus. Traces of this distinction appear in Clement of Alexandria, Pliny, and even certain Manichaean Homilies. We should also note that it appears in the work of one of the most important Ismaili thinkers, Abû Hâtim Râzî (fourth/tenth century). For him, Zaratosht, the Persian Zoroaster, was a dâ’î, a dignitary within the esoteric hierarchy, during the fourth period of the cycle of prophecy, the period of Moses.

Yet despite differences of spelling that merely register variations in pronunciation, the names are, strictly and etymologically speaking, the same. Moreover, the historian Agathias explicitly affirms that Zoroaster and Zaradès are two names for one and the same person. This was also the position of Sohrawardî and the Ishrâqîyûn, to whom the idea of dividing Zoroaster into two separate figures never occurred. Here we encounter a particularly striking kind of perception and representation whose positive meaning escapes us as long as we cannot distinguish what is historically true, in the sense we give that word today, from what is phenomenologically true—true to the way a reality is experienced and disclosed to consciousness.

3) The case of Mânî seems rather more straightforward. We have seen that Sohrawardî speaks of Mânî's “deviation.” Yet several features of his own doctrine and spirituality of Light bear a Manichaean imprint. Perhaps this judgment was, in part, a personal safeguard against those within Islam who knew no more about Mânî's teaching than certain commentators today who indiscriminately speak of “Manichaeism” in matters that have nothing to do with it. Sohrawardî's position is not without parallel. Elsewhere, we have noted the unmistakable and profound traces of Manichaean gnosis within Ismaili gnosis, even though Mânî's name is never mentioned there.

We must always take account of ketmân, the “discipline of secrecy,” the practice of concealing esoteric knowledge. The example of Shahrazôrî, a commentator who was an ishrâqî to the depths of his heart, illustrates this especially well. On the one hand, in the book's prologue, Shahrazôrî summarizes the information then circulating about Mânî: originally a Mazdean, Mânî proposed to combine the Mazdean and Christian religions; he claimed a prophetic mission and preached an asceticism supposedly destined to ruin society. In short, this was the whole stock of conventional opinion, as poorly informed about Manichaeism as Western opinion long remained about the Cathars.

On the other hand, in the section of the Eastern Theosophy dealing with the Last Things, we find an extended discussion by the same Shahrazôrî, in which he presents the teaching not of the impious Mânî but of Mânî the sage (al-Hakîm Mânî), concerning the Column of Light and the Earth of Light. Shahrazôrî relates this teaching to Sohrawardî's doctrine of the imaginal world of the “eighth climate”—the middle or intermediate East, to which we shall shortly return—and concludes: “If this is indeed what the sage Mânî intended by these symbols, as we have just explained them, then his teaching is true.” Otherwise, naturally, it would be false. But Shahrazôrî does not entertain that possibility.

All this seems to complete our understanding of the nature and content of “Eastern knowledge,” by revealing the figures who upheld it in the past. Meanwhile, the frequent use of the words East and Eastern within the technical vocabulary helps to clarify their meaning still further. The esoteric geography of the spiritual worlds places the Jabarût, the universe of the pure cherubic Intelligences (the Angeli intellectuales of Latin Avicennism), above the Malakût, the universe of the Angels-Souls. The latter comprises the higher Malakût of the Angeli caelestes, or heavenly Souls, and the lower Malakût of human souls.

We shall later distinguish the many worlds within these universes (Chapter III). For the moment, let us note that Sohrawardî calls them, respectively, the Greater East, or the farthest spiritual East (al-sharq al-akbar), and the Lesser East (al-sharq al-asghar). The physical, bodily world (molk), the world of visible phenomena (shahâdat), is the West, where souls decline. This will be the central theme of the mystical Tale of the Western Exile (see Chapter VI). It is a spiritual geography already familiar to Avicenna.

In the descending procession of being, the Intelligences “rise” at the East, the horizon of the Godhead, the Light of Lights. The heavenly Souls “rise” at the East that is morning for them: the world of the Intelligences. Human souls descend toward the West of the physical world, into the Darkness of Matter, the “land of exile,” where they must temporarily govern a body of flesh. Conversely, in the ascent back toward the origin (so’ûd, ma’âd), the soul's manifestation outside the physical body—through profound meditation, ecstatic vision, or death—constitutes its rising dawn, its Ishrâq, and its manifestation (tajallî) after a complete katharsis, or purification.

The world of Souls is then revealed to it as its “East.” The soul “rises” at that East by revealing itself to itself, lifting itself above the horizon of the body, which had been its West. Then the world of the Intelligences is revealed to it: the Greater East. The soul “rises” there by ascending beyond the world of Soul, which now becomes like a West in relation to the “Eastern Intelligence” (al-’Aql al-mashriqî).

Besides these two Easts, there is also a “middle” or “intermediate East” (al-sharq al-awsat). This “Middle East” is simply another name for what our philosophers, in contrast to the “seven climates” of traditional geography, call the eighth climate. It is the “second world,” where all the forms, figures, and colors of our own world appear, in even greater richness and diversity, but in a state beyond sensory perception. Here lie the mystical cities of Jâbalqâ, Jâbarsâ, and Hûrqalyâ. This is the whole universe of the Malakût as it “rises” within the world of the Soul. It is therefore the intermediate East between the East of the Soul and the West in which souls had been plunged into darkness. We have already devoted so much attention to this universe elsewhere that we would prefer not to repeat ourselves here.

The essential point is this. Each of the three universes has its own corresponding faculty of perception. The Jabarût is apprehended through intellectual intuition; the Malakût through imaginative intuition; and the physical world through sensory perception, the empirical knowledge provided by the five external senses.

We must emphasize once again that the imaginative faculty, or imagination, directed toward the Malakût must not be confused with what we ordinarily call fantasy. It is a genuine faculty of knowledge, with its own distinctive power of understanding, and the world it perceives possesses reality in its own right. Sohrawardî appears to have been the first to establish systematically the particular ontology, the distinct order of being, proper to this intermediate universe. This obliges us to abandon the adjective “imaginary” when referring to the mundus imaginalis (’âlam al-mithâl). Elsewhere, we have proposed calling it the imaginal world.

Thus the jism mithâlî, the subtle body, is an imaginal body, not an “imaginary” one. Knowledge of the imaginal world, or intermediate East, is itself an “Eastern” knowledge. Sensory perception, by contrast, and the fantasy that produces what is merely “imaginary,” are “Western” forms of knowledge.

The imaginal world fulfills an indispensable function. It frees us from the dilemma so often posed today when spiritual events are discussed: myth or history? The events of the intermediate East are neither one nor the other. They belong to a world with events of its own. It is in this intermediate East, this “eighth climate,” that the Revelations given to the prophets come into being, that the events of sacred history unfold, and that the happenings described in visionary narratives take place. There too occur the manifestations of the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, and finally the event of the Resurrection (qiyâmat), the prelude to future renewals of life. Sohrawardî rightly observes that no philosophy which denies itself this intermediate world can understand the language of Ishrâq.
